extracted.intended_audience: instructional designers, online educators, and researchers in distance education
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for selecting, designing, and evaluating media and modes for online/distance learning (print, graphics, audio, video, mobile, Internet/Web2.0/3.0), with attention to pedagogy, learner differences, and technical constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimedia principle (Mayer #1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multimedia principle: Students learn better from words with graphics or pictures than from words alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use graphics alongside words to improve learning; prefer combined verbal and visual presentation rather than text-only delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spatial contiguity principle (Mayer #2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spatial contiguity principle: Students learn better when corresponding words and pictures are presented closer to each other on the page or screen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place labels/captions adjacent to related graphics; avoid separating explanatory text from the visuals it describes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal contiguity principle (Mayer #3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporal contiguity principle: Students learn better when corresponding words and pictures are presented simultaneously rather than successively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Synchronize narration/text with animations or visuals so learners receive related verbal and visual information at the same time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence principle (Mayer #4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coherence principle: Students learn better when extraneous words, pictures, and sounds are excluded rather than included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminate irrelevant decorative graphics, music, or verbiage that do not support learning objectives to reduce cognitive load.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modality principle (Mayer #5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modality principle: Students learn better from animation and audible narration than from animation and on-screen text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer spoken narration with animation rather than displaying the same text on-screen; leverage audio narration to complement visuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redundancy principle (Mayer #6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Redundancy principle: People have a limited capacity to process visual and auditory material presented simultaneously; therefore, students learn better from animation and narration than from a combination of animation, narration, and on-screen text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid simultaneously presenting identical on-screen text and narration with animation; excess redundant channels can impede learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual differences principle (Mayer #7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual differences principle: Design effects are stronger for low-knowledge learners than for high-knowledge learners, and for high-spatial-ability learners than for low-spatial-ability learners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt multimedia design to learner prior knowledge and spatial ability; expect differential effects and provide options when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize course design and pedagogy over media
rubrics_metrics.description: Course design and pedagogy are always more important than media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose media to serve instructional goals and pedagogy; do not assume a technologically elegant medium is inherently appropriate for all contexts or audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust interaction to individual needs
rubrics_metrics.description: All interaction is not equally useful; interaction should be adjusted to individual needs and preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess learner preferences (e.g., field-dependence, maturity, autonomy) and provide varying forms and amounts of interaction and instructor support accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching presence as essential design criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching presence is the leadership and facilitation necessary for individuals to achieve 'meaningful understanding' through interaction and collaboration; includes design and organization, discourse facilitation, and direct instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructor/moderator must provide appropriate amounts of structure, discourse facilitation, and direct instruction to scaffold collaboration and guide learners who may not spontaneously engage productively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learner activity with media matters more than teacher's activity
rubrics_metrics.description: What the learner does with media is more important than what the teacher does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate media by the learning activities they afford (collaboration, autonomy, practice) rather than by novelty or instructor actions alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor technical competence over teaching experience
rubrics_metrics.description: In terms of student learning outcomes, the teaching experience of the instructor does not matter as much as the instructor’s experience with technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize instructor/media-competence and provide training/support to ensure effective technology-mediated instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure requirement for less-experienced learners
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure in the learning environment is usually plentiful in face-to-face situations and potentially essential where sound study skills or habits may be lacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear organization, sequencing, and scaffolded activities especially for undergraduates, novices, or learners with weaker study skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for learner characteristics (maturity, literacy, styles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Learners differ in desire/capacity for autonomy, self-direction, and required skills (e.g., ability to explain ideas in text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design for varied maturity levels, literacy, and communication styles; include compensating media-based assistance (e.g., supports for text production).

rubrics_metrics.name: Print/text: affordances and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Print strengths: low cost, flexibility, portability, stability, convenience for instruction and feedback. Weaknesses: static, may reduce involvement, relatively non-interactive, slower/costlier to revise, may lead to passive learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use print/text where affordability, portability and stable reference are priorities; supplement with multimedia where interactivity, engagement, or rapid revision is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphics principle: emphasize critical details and avoid extraneous visuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Visuals that emphasize critical details relevant to learning are most effective; unnecessary visuals may be distracting, especially for learners with limited attention or discrimination skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor simple, focused diagrams over ornate or highly realistic imagery unless added detail is pedagogically necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphics principle: include supporting captions and avoid assuming self-explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagrams, charts, and graphs should not be assumed self-explanatory; graphics should include clearly written supporting captions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concise captions and labels to make the instructional purpose of visuals explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour use guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Colour may increase search speed but can distract; recommended vivid colours include green, cyan, white, and yellow; end-users should be able to control colour given colour-blindness; best combinations are blue/black/red on white or white/yellow/green on black.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid excessive colours; design for accessibility (contrast, user control) and for mid-range displays rather than assuming high-end hardware.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screen/display design guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider display area limitations (PC screen ~1/3 page), top-left priority for important information, single-colour high-contrast backgrounds (white/off-white best), avoid textured backgrounds, use sans serif fonts with mixed case, choose font size by purpose (12–14pt for reading), use font changes sparingly and avoid colour-only emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design for common, mid-range equipment and apply these legibility/layout rules sparingly to preserve emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Videoconferencing pedagogic characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Videoconferencing adds a sense of direct involvement and presence, can provide quality learning opportunities and delivery of global expertise to remote learners, and can reduce travel time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit live interaction to foster presence and deliver demonstrations, but be mindful of cost and accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Videoconference design critical issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical issues in video-based training include: proper training of instructors; user self-consciousness; integration of other media; optimum length of sessions & group size; session variety; technical design and support; professional quality visual elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address these operational and pedagogic factors when planning video sessions to ensure effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Videoconferencing strengths for learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Strengths include fostering social presence and cohesion, permitting sharing of visual resources, making collaborative learning feasible, and helping teach abstract, time-protracted, hazardous, or unfamiliar concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use videoconferencing strategically for relationship-building, demonstrations, and scenarios unsuited to other media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audio pedagogic effects and best uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Audio can aid recall (summaries), offer learner control when asynchronous (podcasts, iPods), provide a familiar human voice, be motivating when combined with text, and be valuable in language/music instruction and accessibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use audio where voice, portability, or learner control adds value; weigh benefits against storage/bandwidth/costs and allow learner choice of using audio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audio cautions and empirical findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning gains from one-way audio alone are weak; high-verbal-skill learners often gain little from adding audio to text; audio may lengthen instruction time; audio quality depends on compression/bandwidth; synthesized speech increases cognitive load.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid default use of audio unless pedagogically justified; monitor quality and let learners opt in/out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match media mix to relationship-building vs information-exchange goals (Picard)
rubrics_metrics.description: When needs for relationship-building and information exchange are both low, audio alone may suffice; when both are high, audio, video, and data (including text) should all be present; relationship building is enhanced by combining audio, video, and data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select combinations (audio/data/video) based on whether the objective is building relationships, exchanging information, or both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobile/PDAs constraints and implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Mobile devices (PDAs, smartphones) can deliver video and multimedia but require high bandwidth; display area and device memory constrain design; design should consider device size and likely network/bandwidth limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optimize content for small screens, lower bandwidth, and provide formats appropriate to mobile storage/processing limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet as medium: affordances and weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: The Internet links participants and information, supports tailoring and collaboration, but can lack structure, cause navigation problems, be non-interactive in Web 1.0 forms, have variable reliability, and requires learner literacy and computer skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide organization, navigation aids, and scaffolding when using the Web; design for learner skill levels and beware one-way Web content that lacks interactivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Web 2.0/3.0 affordances for online learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Web 2.0 (tagging, social networks, user-generated content like wikis/blogs/podcasts) supports learner creation and collaboration; Web 3.0 (Semantic Web) promises machine-readable labeling and improved retrieval but requires widespread metadata standardization and mobile broadband.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage Web2.0 tools to enable learner-generated content and community; plan for possible Semantic-Web benefits while recognizing infrastructure and metadata challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infrastructure and policy considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: New Internets and network initiatives are motivated by needs for security, manageability, speed, and accessibility; growth depends on ease-of-use, power/speed, cost, and accessible content; governments may have responsibility to fund/maintain research networks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning large-scale or research education projects, consider network architecture, funding, and policy constraints as part of media selection and deployment.
